1:
The superscription has defeated everyone who tried it, and most of them say so. Henry calls the title a very uncertain sound, referred by some to the death of Goliath, by others of Nabal or Absalom, and inclines to think it names only a tune or an instrument, taking the enemies in view to be the nations that opposed David's settlement on the throne. Calvin lists the same options and judges it more probable that the words are the opening of a well-known song to whose tune the psalm was set. Clarke gathers the versions: the Chaldee reads it of the death of the strong man who went out between the camps, the Vulgate and the Greek and the Ethiopic of the secrets of the Son, the Arabic of the mysteries of the Son and his resurrection; Houbigant forced the Hebrew into agreement with those by joining two words into one meaning hidden things, a division about a hundred manuscripts and printed editions share. Some read instead the infancy of the Son, which is how several of the fathers came to take the title of the incarnation; Clarke thinks it as painful as useless to follow every conjecture. Delitzsch is blunter: he calls Luther's beautiful youth bolder still and rules both renderings out, the preposition occurring only once in the text, and traces the Nabal reading, revived by Hengstenberg as a collective name for all Nabal-like fools, to the same erroneous idea. Ellicott notes only that the alphabetic arrangement begins here in its completest form, every clause of the first stanza opening with Aleph.

What whole-hearted praise means is the second question, and the voices press it one way. Gill identifies the vow with what the New Testament calls making melody in the heart, but insists the verb means to confess, to declare openly in the public congregation, so that this is vocal singing with the heart joining and not mere mental singing; and he knows how rarely it happens, God sometimes having nothing of the heart in worship and sometimes only a share, divided with the creature. Calvin takes the whole heart for an upright heart against a double one, and turns it into an indictment: irreligious men are ashamed to defraud God of praise outright, but no sooner have they uttered one acknowledgement than they begin to sing triumphs to their own valour, which is pure mockery, since after making their oblation they sacrifice to their own counsels and skill and courage. The generals of antiquity who had thanksgivings decreed in their names abused them under a false pretence, to get an opportunity for boasting. God cannot bear, Calvin says, to see his glory appropriated by the creature in even the smallest degree. Spurgeon puts the argument in four words, that half heart is no heart, and adds that our thanks must have long wings and mount aloft to heaven, however grateful we are to the intermediate agent.

Where the gladness finally rests is the third point. Henry has the joy pass through whatever occasions it and terminate in God only, not in the gift so much as in the giver, and reads one mercy as the occasion for remembering former ones. Spurgeon says the same in his own coin: gratitude for one mercy refreshes the memory as to thousands of others, one silver link in the chain drawing up a long series of tender remembrances. Gill lists what the rejoicing is not in, neither riches nor warlike exploits nor horses and chariots, but in the Lord as the God of all grace, the Chaldee making its object the Word. Calvin uses the same backward look to explain the psalm's shape: it is a mistake to tie this thanksgiving to one victory, since by recalling many deliverances the psalmist encourages himself to expect help in the trouble now upon him, and so opens the gate of prayer.
3:
The turning back of the enemies is read first as grammar. Ellicott renders it literally, in the turning of mine enemies back, and allows it to mean when they turned or because they turned or both, the older versions having chosen when; he joins it to the preceding verse as one sentence and prefers stumble through weakness to fall, following the Greek. Gill fills the clause with instances instead: the Philistines turned back when their champion was dead, the men who came to apprehend Christ went backwards and fell to the ground, and sin and Satan and at last antichrist retreat from the Lord's people, stumbling at whatever Providence throws in their way and perishing as wax melts before fire. Clarke turns it inward: when sin begins to lose its power through being resisted, that is the sign of a nearly approaching conquest, and the time to follow on to know the Lord.

The vindication in the next verse is a courtroom scene, furnished differently by each voice. Gill has God plead and defend the cause, proving by the flight and ruin of the enemies that it was just. Ellicott notes that the Hebrew says thou hast made my judgment, as the Greek and the Latin have it, and reaches for Shakespeare on the Judge whom no king can corrupt. Delitzsch reads the verse structurally: this is the gimel strophe, perhaps standing for the two letters that follow as well, continuing the ground of thanksgiving already laid down, since the psalmist celebrates not the one judicial act he has just experienced but that act as the sum of many before it.

Who exactly was rebuked and blotted out is the first real dispute, and nobody agrees. Gill reports the Targum and Kimchi for the Philistines and others for Amalek, then refers the verse to Gospel times and the rebuke of the heathen by preaching, and above all to the latter day and the antichristian states. Clarke admits we cannot know what is meant and guesses the Canaanitish nations, but turns the phrase into an argument: for ever and ever here has its proper sense of endless, and whoever insists it means a limited time may tell us where the Hivites and Perizzites now dwell. Delitzsch, following Hengstenberg, would have the Amalekites in view beside the Ammonites, threatened since the time of Moses with a blotting out of their remembrance, and calls the threatening the word of omnipotence that destroys as against the word that creates. Ellicott keeps to the register: blotted out is better than put out, and means the family extinct and its name erased from the civil roll. He also notes that the Daleth stanza is missing.

The last verse of the stanza is obscure if not corrupt, and two of the four refuse the received reading. Ellicott says flatly that the vocative gives no intelligible meaning and renders it as a statement, the enemy made an utter wreck and perpetual ruin, desolations coming from a word meaning to be dried up; the Greek and Latin read with a sound, which he takes for the crash of falling cities. He will not let anyone substitute enemies for cities: the emphasis falls on the evanishment of great cities from history as a sign of judgment, so that the poet probably thinks of Sodom and Gomorrha, and we of the mounds that alone represent Nineveh and Babylon. Clarke re-renders it to the same effect, noting that Canaanite cities have perished so utterly that neither name nor vestige remains. Gill alone keeps the address and asks who is meant, dismissing Goliath because no destroyed cities are recorded of him, reporting Jarchi for Esau and others for Amalek, and settling on antichrist rather than Satan. Delitzsch makes the contrast the strophe's point: the enemies vanish without a trace of remembrance, while the Lord abides enthroned for ever, and abides as Judge.
7:
Against the vanished cities stands a throne that does not vanish. Ellicott would render the line not as endurance but as enthronement, Jehovah sits enthroned for ever, in close parallelism with the clause that follows, for judgment has erected his throne. Gill reads the verb the same way and glosses it from a Jewish writer as sitting in rest and quiet, takes it for the unchangeableness and power of God, notes that the Chaldee makes the subject the Word of the Lord whose habitation is in the highest heavens, and applies the whole to Christ, who sits King for ever until his enemies are made his footstool. Wesley states the contrast plainly: cities and people may perish, but the Lord abides, which is enough for the terror of his enemies and the comfort of his church. Spurgeon draws the inference about time, that in the light of the past the future is not doubtful, since the same Almighty fills the throne of power.

That the throne is prepared for judgment sets Spurgeon thinking about court delays. He takes the preparation for the swiftness of divine justice: in heaven's court no suitor is worn out by waiting, the term lasts all the year round, and though thousands come at once neither plaintiff nor defendant can complain of a cause not fairly heard. Partiality and respect of persons, he adds, are unknown in the dealings of the Holy One of Israel, and so impartial a tribunal should check us when tempted and comfort us when slandered. Gill fixes the scope: the word rendered world is, as Ben Melech observes, a general name for all the countries of the habitable earth, which shows the universal judgment is meant. Clarke makes it a rule about providence as a whole, that all its dispensations are founded in righteousness and truth. Ellicott marks only the emphatic pronoun, and he it is who.

The same judge is a fortress for the crushed, and the lexical work here is where the voices add most. Delitzsch explains that the word is a high steep place out of reach of danger, a figure David knew from his time of persecution, and that the oppressed are properly those broken in pieces, pulverised, overwhelmed to the point of being completely crushed. Ellicott agrees on both words, calling the refuge a citadel into which the persecuted would retreat, and traces trouble to a root meaning to be cut off from something, provisions or water, whose cognate elsewhere means drought. Gill supplies the list of oppressions the word has to carry, the burden of sin, Satan's temptations, the persecutions of men, and being trodden under foot by antichrist, and finds the figure already given in the law, since the cities of refuge were where the manslayer fled from the avenger of blood. Spurgeon puts that in one line: there were cities of refuge under the law, and God is our refuge-city under the gospel.

Knowing the name is what turns the fortress into a place anyone would run to. Ellicott makes the name itself a watchword of strength and protection, which is why those who know it trust it, and derives the verb for seeking from a root meaning to tread or frequent a place, possibly with allusion to frequenting the Temple courts. Wesley takes the name for infinite power and wisdom and faithfulness and goodness, observes that the name of God is frequently put for God, and finds the ground of confidence in the experience of his faithfulness to his people in all ages. Clarke wants the knowledge experimental rather than reported, an acquaintance with mercy that carries the conviction that God never has forsaken and never will forsake those who trust him. Gill presses the same distinction hardest, allowing neither a merely notional and speculative knowledge nor a professional one, but only the knowledge that is affectionate, spiritual and experimental.
11:
Having praised God by himself, the psalmist turns and recruits. Henry reads the turn as characteristic: those who believe God is greatly to be praised want others brought to the work, and would gladly be instrumental in bringing them. He makes the dwelling in Zion the hinge: the special residence of God's glory is in heaven and of his grace in his church, of which Zion was a type, and there he meets his people with his promises and expects to be met with their praises, so that in all our praising we should have an eye to him as specially present in the assemblies of his people, their protector and patron. The summons runs two ways: to his own subjects, for the honour of God and of their country and religion, and to his neighbours, that they might sing praises not to their false gods but to the God of Israel. Gill agrees that the Lord may be praised by celebrating the perfections of his nature and by living to his glory, but insists the word here means praise sung by a modulation of the voice in musical notes, the same word used of the singing of birds, and sung by the saints in concert, as Paul and Silas sang in prison. Wesley adds only that Zion is where the gracious presence is, the people addressed being the heathen nations. Clarke turns the verse into a rebuke of his own readers: those who have received salvation ought to recommend it to the whole circle of their acquaintance, yet Christians so called, when they meet, seldom speak about God, because they have nothing to say.

The ground of the summons is an inquisition, and Ellicott identifies the figure precisely. The clause is better read as a reason, for he maketh inquisition, the Hebrew literally calling God the seeker of bloods, the avenger of blood; the allusion is to the goel, the nearest relative of a murdered man, bound by Oriental custom to avenge him. He puts the verbs in the past, remembered and forgot not, and prefers the afflicted to the humble, the two readings being forms of one root commonly distinguished as ethical and physical, a distinction he says Biblical usage does not bear out. Gill reports the Arabic, which makes God remember the man who seeks their blood rather than the blood itself, and applies it to the one made drunk with the blood of the martyrs; but he prefers to read God as searching for the blood of his saints, which he knows wherever it was privily shed, as he knew Abel's, the searching showing his strict care. Clarke widens the charge from the neighbours of Israel to every nation that has made destructive wars to enlarge its territory or extend its commerce: for the blood such nations have shed their own shall be shed, and if man makes no inquisition for it, God will. Wesley grants the delay and denies the forgetfulness, since the authors of that bloodshed will certainly be called to a severe account.

What the remembering amounts to is Henry's closing theme. God makes inquisition by his judgments on earth before he makes it by the judgment of the great day, remembering every drop of innocent blood and returning it sevenfold on the head of the bloodthirsty, giving them blood to drink, for they are worthy. A day is coming, Henry says, when what was shed secretly will be discovered and what was shed unjustly avenged; then it will appear how precious the blood of his people is to him, and that he has forgotten neither the cry of their blood nor the cry of their prayers, both being sealed up among his treasures. Clarke ends from the other side, with the cry of a humbled people driven to distraction and ruin by such wars, which is not forgotten before him.
13:
The psalm turns from celebration to petition, and Spurgeon notices what carried it there: memories of the past and confidences about the future brought the man to the mercy seat to plead for the needs of the present, so that between praising and praying he divided all his time, and it is hard to see how he could have spent it more profitably. The petition itself he admires as a model, suitable for all persons and occasions, breathing a humble spirit, showing self-knowledge, and appealing to the right attributes and the right person. As some texts have been called little Bibles, he says, this sentence may be called a little prayer-book, for it holds the soul and marrow of prayer; it is much in little, it turns every way like the angelic sword, and though the ladder looks short it reaches from earth to heaven. Gill draws the doctrine out of it: a man already called by grace and already shown mercy still needs more, fresh discoveries of pardoning grace, merciful supplies, merciful support, merciful deliverances from enemies inward and outward, and such a man flees to God rather than the creature, pleading neither his own dignity nor his righteousness nor his merit but only mercy. Clarke sets the verse in the psalm's argument, where David, having laid down the preceding maxims, now claims his own part in their truth.

Two sets of gates frame the request, and the commentators keep them firmly apart. Clarke makes the first an open grave leading to a yawning hell, and the second all the ordinances of God by which a soul is helped forward to heaven. Wesley reads the second as the great assemblies, elegantly opposed to the first, and explains the daughter as the people who live and meet together in the city, since cities are as it were mothers to their people and their people are commonly called their daughters, as the daughters of Egypt and Edom and Tyre stand for the inhabitants of those places. Spurgeon dwells on the title rather than the gates, calling it a glorious lift: in sickness, in sin, in despair, in temptation we have been brought very low and the gloomy portal has seemed about to open and imprison us, yet underneath were the everlasting arms, and we have been raised as far as the gates of heaven. He borrows Trapp's quaint way of putting it, that God commonly reserves his hand for a dead lift and rescues those who were already talking of their graves. Delitzsch states the reversal as the reason the church can praise at all: it has been rescued from death, and those who wanted death to overtake it have fallen a prey to death themselves.

Why the mercy is wanted matters as much as that it is wanted. Spurgeon will not let the stated purpose be overlooked, since the object is God's glory and not relief: the saints are not so selfish as to look only to themselves, but desire mercy's diamond so that others may see it flash and sparkle and admire the giver of such priceless gems. Gill measures the promise honestly. All thy praise can only mean as many of the bounties and acts of goodness deserving praise as the psalmist had experience of and was capable of observing, because the instances of divine grace are so many that in the present state of things they cannot be reckoned up in order, nor God praised for them as he should be. Clarke keeps the two gates in one sentence, so that being saved from the one is precisely what puts a man in the other with something to say.
15:
The praise promised earlier now actually begins, and Gill says so: this, as Jarchi and Aben Ezra observe, is the praise he had determined to show forth, occasioned by the destruction of God's enemies and the deliverance of his people. He will not let the heathen be the Philistines, as Kimchi reads them, who meant to make Israel fall and fell themselves, but takes the verse prophetically of the nations that joined in the idolatry of antichrist and of the states to be destroyed at Armageddon, noting that the metaphor comes from hunters who dig pits for wild beasts. Spurgeon works the same image and finds the justice of it in its economy: God makes the wicked their own executioners, since these cunning hunters prepared a pitfall for the godly and fell in themselves, the victim's foot escaping while the toils closed on those who set them, so that a snare laboriously made proved its efficacy by catching its own maker. He generalises without softening it: persecutors are often ruined by their own malicious projects, drunkards kill themselves, prodigals beggar themselves, the contentious are involved in ruinous costs, the envious eat their own hearts and blasphemers curse their souls.

That God is known by the judgment he executes is read as a statement about his character before it is read as a statement about events. Spurgeon puts the argument first: the punishment of sin is required by what God is, since his holiness and abhorrence of sin are displayed in judging, and a ruler who winked at evil would soon be known by all his subjects to be evil himself, while one severely just in judgment reveals his own nature in it. So long as God is God, he says, he cannot spare the guilty, except through that one glorious way in which he is just and yet the justifier of him that believes. Clarke enters a caution against reading judgments too readily, since not every casualty can properly be called one: judgment is God's strange work, and when he does execute it his mind is plainly to be seen, there being no natural causes to which such calamities can legally be attributed. He adds the other half as a weighty truth, that nothing a wicked man does is not against his own interest, and that he takes more pains to destroy his soul than the righteous man takes to have his saved. Ellicott recasts the whole line as two finished clauses, Jehovah hath made himself known, he hath executed judgment, snaring the wicked in the work of his own hands. Gill reads the coming judgment on antichrist as a just retaliation, measured out in kind: as he killed with the sword his followers shall be killed with the sword, as he led captive he shall be taken captive, as he burnt the martyrs he shall be cast into the lake of fire.

The two untranslated words that close the stanza divide the voices between music and meditation. Ellicott observes that where the first is translated elsewhere it comes out once as meditation and once as solemn sound; both senses are etymologically possible, but he thinks it marks some change in the music, or perhaps, joined with the second word, a direction to one part of the orchestra. Wesley leaves it open between a musical term and a note of attention, intimating that the matter deserves consideration. Clarke takes both at once, telling his reader to meditate on this and mark it well, and reporting the view that the words direct the players, like the tempo marks of his own day telling them to play briskly and boldly and let sense and sound accompany each other. Spurgeon treats them as a summons to the reader rather than the band: meditate, pause, consider and tune your instrument, adjusting your hearts to a solemnity that becomes the subject.
17:
Where the wicked are said to go divides the voices, and the division is a translation before it is a doctrine. Ellicott calls the received rendering most unfortunate: the verb is to return, not to be turned, as the Greek and Latin have it, and the destination is the grave, the dust of the original doom, or the unseen world; the verbs may even be imperative, let them return. He ties the verse to the one before it, since the wicked bring about their own destruction and so bear witness to the righteous judgment of Jehovah, and grants the word its force, a double sign of direction carrying the sense right down to the world of death. Gill knows that rendering and rejects it, since returning to dust is common to all men, righteous and wicked alike; he takes the place named to be the place of torment where devils and damned spirits are, to which the souls of the wicked go immediately on leaving their bodies and to which they will be remanded in soul and body after the judgment, their damnation being everlasting separation from God. True of all the wicked, he says, but chiefly meant of antichrist and his followers. Clarke keeps the traditional sense and presses the emphasis of the original: headlong into hell, down into hell.

The second half of the verse widens the warning, and the voices take it personally. Clarke distinguishes forgetting from ignorance: there are nations and individuals who know God and are nevertheless unmindful of him, not acknowledging him in their designs or works, and these are all to be thrust down; he then turns on his reader, asking whether he is forgetful of his Maker and of him who died for him. Wesley defines the forgetting as not regarding God, nor his precepts, nor his threatenings. Spurgeon finds the verse the most solemn in the psalm and spells out who is caught by it: the moral who are not devout, the honest who are not prayerful, the benevolent who are not believing, the amiable who are not converted must all have their portion with the openly wicked, and whole nations are of that kind, forgetters of God being far more numerous than the profligate. Forgetfulness looks a small sin, he says, yet it brings eternal wrath on the man who lives and dies in it.

Against that stands the promise to the needy, and Ellicott notes that the negative stands emphatically at the head of the Hebrew, governing both clauses: the sufferer's hope of being righted will be realised, and in that confidence the psalmist summons Jehovah as judge. Delitzsch reads the same movement, the prayer growing more confident about what is still threatened because an act of judgment has already been witnessed. Gill keeps both halves of the experience. The people of God are poor and needy for the most part, poor in temporal things and poor in spirit, and strictly speaking are never forgotten, being engraven on his hands and set as a seal on his heart; yet they may seem forgotten to themselves and others, and remain so a long time, the holy city trodden under foot and the witnesses prophesying in sackcloth. Clarke accounts for the delay instead of denying it: deliverance is deferred for the greater confusion of their enemies, the greater manifestation of mercy, and their own benefit. Spurgeon answers the fear in its own terms: mercy is as ready to her work as justice ever is, and if the needy fear they are forgotten, let them rejoice that they shall not always be so; where Satan tells poor tremblers their hope shall perish, they have the assurance that their expectation shall not perish for ever. The Lord's people, he adds, are a humbled people, emptied and sensible of need, driven to a daily attendance on God: they may wait, but not in vain.
19:
The psalm ends where it was heading, in petition. Gill reads the summons as double, to the destruction of the enemies and the salvation of the people, and Clarke turns it into a date, asking that this be the time the oppressed and persecuted are delivered. Ellicott sharpens the next clause: let not mere man be defiant. Spurgeon builds his comment on the military figure: prayers are the believer's weapons of war, and when the battle is too hard we call in our great ally, who lies as it were in ambush until faith gives the signal by crying Arise. A cause all but lost, he says, is soon won again if the Almighty does but bestir himself, who will not suffer man to prevail over God but confounds their gloryings with swift judgments; and when the wicked are punished in his very sight, he who is now all tenderness will have no compassion, since they had no tears of repentance while their day of grace endured.

The last petition is textually uncertain, and the grammarian parts company with the expositors over it. Ellicott states the difficulty plainly: the Greek, the Latin and the Syriac all read place a lawgiver over them, and Hitzig conjectured set a guard upon them, while the received text apparently yields put a terror upon them, a proof of power enough to trouble and subdue them. Clarke commits himself to the other reading and renders the Hebrew as a prayer for a teacher to be placed among them, that they may learn they too are accountable creatures; he notes that though several manuscripts have fear, teacher or legislator is the reading of every version but one, and collects two older English renderings that caught it, one setting a schoolmaster over them and one a bringer of law above them. Gill keeps the received reading and prays for fear to be injected into a bold and fearless generation who, like the unjust judge, neither fear God nor regard men, expecting it at the destruction of Babylon, when kings and merchants stand afar off for fear of her torment.

What the nations are to learn is that they are but men, and the preachers press it. Clarke makes it evangelical, that the Gentiles be taught by preaching that they are weak and helpless and need the salvation Christ has provided, and reads the closing note as a direction to mark it well. Spurgeon finds the vanity astonishing and the cure educational: one would think men would not grow so vain as to deny being men, yet it seems a lesson only a divine schoolmaster can teach proud spirits. Crowns leave their wearers but men, he says, degrees of eminent learning make their owners no more than men, valour and conquest cannot raise anyone off that dead level, and the wealth of Croesus and the wisdom of Solon and the power of Alexander together would still leave their possessor a man.

Clarke closes by quoting Horsley's three-part division of the psalm, which doubles as a reading of its temperature. The first ten verses are prophetic of the utter extermination of the irreligious persecuting faction, delivered as a song of victory in which the psalmist, in the height of prophetic enthusiasm, speaks of the threatened vengeance as accomplished. The second opens by exhorting God's people to praise him as the avenger of their wrongs, then lowers the strain, mixing the notes of triumph with supplication and complaint as the mind flutters between things present and to come. In the third the psalmist seems returned from that enthusiasm to his natural state, closing with explicit but cool assertions of the destruction of the wicked and the deliverance of the persecuted. Spurgeon ends with an exercise rather than a summary: read the psalm again as the triumphal hymn of the Redeemer laying the glory of his victories at his Father's feet.
